tldr: Moving beyond the conventional constraint of keeping the ultrasound probe strictly normal to the body surface, this work introduces an omni-directional orientation control framework. Powered by real-time quadratic surface modeling with dual end-effector RGB-D cameras, it accurately maintains and tracks non-normal probe tilt angles—crucial for clinical imaging—even during respiratory motion.
hero_caption: Overall workflow and the three-stage experimental validation of the proposed system. (a) Fusing surface point clouds from dual end-effector RGB-D cameras and estimating the local surface normal and target tilt angle via quadratic surface fitting. (b) Angle-tracking accuracy evaluation on a flat plate. (c) Target-view search and posture recovery on a cardiac phantom. (d) In-vivo tracking experiment during respiratory motion on a human subject.
overview:
Medical ultrasound (US) is a vital imaging modality offering real-time visualization without ionizing radiation. However, image quality depends heavily on how the probe is positioned and tilted against the body, placing high technical demands and physical strain on sonographers. While robotic ultrasound systems (RUS) aim to automate these exams, most existing setups can only perform "self-normal-positioning," holding the probe perpendicular to the local skin surface.

Yet real clinical procedures—such as capturing the apical or subcostal 4-chamber (S4C) views in echocardiography—require holding a non-normal tilt angle to peer beneath the ribs or acoustic windows like the liver. Moreover, because breathing causes the body surface to move, fixing probe angles in the robot base frame is not enough. The robot must continuously preserve a target tilt relative to the moving body surface.

To tackle this, the authors mounted two close-range RGB-D cameras on the robot end-effector. They built a pipeline that fits a quadratic surface to local skin point clouds in real time, yielding accurate, low-noise surface normals. In addition, they proposed a task-space controller that encodes target orientations relative to the normal. This controller tracks out-of-plane tilt while ensuring consistent image planes (locking rotation around the probe axis) and stable contact force.

The framework was validated across three stages: tracking target angles on a flat plate, autonomously searching for and recovering an S4C view on a cardiac phantom, and continuously tracking an S4C view on a volunteer during free breathing. Results showed a mean angular tracking error of 1.06°, sustained deep tilt angles up to about 44°, and robust acquisition of diagnostic ultrasound images adapting to respiratory surface motion.
contributions: Formulated a local surface modeling method using dual close-range RGB-D point cloud fusion and quadratic surface fitting, delivering fast, low-noise normal estimation even on curved and uneven body surfaces.

Designed an omni-directional probe orientation control law that extends conventional self-normal-positioning to track arbitrary target angles relative to the surface normal, while simultaneously enforcing in-plane orthogonality, axial rotation constraints, and contact force regulation.

Demonstrated clinical feasibility across three experimental benchmarks: flat-surface tracking (1.06° mean error), autonomous S4C view search and angle recovery on a cardiac phantom, and in-vivo S4C view tracking under respiratory motion.

sections.heading: Why "Just Pushing Perpendicularly" Fails in the Clinic
sections.summary: In robotic ultrasound, controlling probe orientation is essential for diagnostic image quality. However, most previous systems focused solely on keeping the probe perpendicular to the skin, creating an intrinsic gap with real clinical exams that require angled views.
sections.details:
Medical ultrasound is a safe, radiation-free, real-time diagnostic tool, but image quality is highly sensitive to probe orientation and contact. Over time, prolonged scanning often causes work-related musculoskeletal disorders among sonographers. Robotic ultrasound systems (RUS) have been pursued to ease this physical burden and standardize image acquisition.

A key hurdle in robotic scanning is precise probe orientation control. Even minor angular deviations can cause the target anatomy to drop out or degrade image quality. Crucially, most prior studies focused only on "self-normal-positioning"—holding the probe perpendicular to the body surface. In routine clinical practice, such as acquiring the subcostal 4-chamber (S4C) view in echocardiography, sonographers must tilt the probe steeply upward from below the xiphoid process toward the heart, aiming through the acoustic window of the abdominal wall and liver.

Past attempts have used passive mechanical joints, force-sensor-based normal estimation, or external RGB-D cameras. Yet these approaches often introduced bulky end-effectors, sensitivity to contact noise, and line-of-sight occlusions. The authors previously proposed an Active-Sensing End-Effector (A-SEE) using close-range RGB-D cameras; however, it relied on simple nearest-neighbor normal estimation, which degraded on curved anatomy, and it was restricted to surface-normal alignment. This work radically upgrades that geometric modeling pipeline and expands the control paradigm to omni-directional tracking at arbitrary non-normal angles.

sections.heading: Achieving Arbitrary Tilt via Quadratic Fitting and Task-Space Control
sections.summary: By fusing point clouds from dual end-effector RGB-D cameras, local surface geometry is modeled using quadratic fitting in just ~0.1 ms. The desired imaging direction is represented as a relative rotation from the estimated normal, driving a task-space controller that balances in-plane contact, image-plane locking, and force control.
sections.details:
The primary control objective is to align the probe's approach vector with a clinically defined target vector $v_d$ relative to the surface normal. Meanwhile, the controller must satisfy an in-plane orthogonality constraint ($\theta_{in}$) to preserve acoustic contact and enforce zero axial angular velocity ($\dot{\theta}_{ax} = 0$) to keep the anatomical cross-section stable.

[Dual RGB-D Perception Pipeline]
Two Intel RealSense D405 cameras (sensing range 7–50 cm) mounted on the end-effector capture local skin point clouds on both sides of the probe. After background masking, the clouds are transformed and fused into a single point cloud $P_w$ in the robot base frame, avoiding self-occlusion from the probe body.

[Quadratic Surface Modeling]
To accommodate steep body curvatures, a quadratic surface $z(x, y) = a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 y + a_3 x^2 + a_4 xy + a_5 y^2$ is fitted to the fused points via least squares. This formulation offers two major benefits: it acts as a spatial low-pass filter against high-frequency sensor noise, and it lets the system compute the analytical normal $n_s$ at the probe contact point remarkably fast (0.100–0.123 ms/frame). Point clouds update at 26–29 Hz, ensuring ample speed for real-time control.

[Omni-Directional Tilt Tracking and Arm Control]
The target probe orientation is stored using an axis-angle representation (Rodrigues' rotation formula) as a relative rotation $R_{ns} \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ between the estimated normal $n_s$ and the desired approach vector $a_{des}$. If the normal $n_s(t)$ shifts due to patient breathing, the base-frame target axis $a_{des}(t) = R_{ns} (-n_s(t))$ is recomputed in real time. The orientation controller outputs an angular velocity command $\omega_b$ containing a primary task (approach axis alignment) and a secondary null-space task (axial rotation correction). For translation, a PD force controller tracking $F_{des}$ uses torque-sensor-derived contact force, and commands are mapped to 7-DOF joint velocities via the robot Jacobian pseudo-inverse.

captions.P5: Comparison of local surface modeling methods. (a)–(c) Point cloud fitting examples on a flat plate, human abdomen, and forearm. (d) The quadratic surface model (red) yields substantially lower fitting RMSE than the planar model (green), reducing error by 77.9% on the forearm. (e) Temporal normal estimation variation in static conditions is tightly bounded at 0.32°–1.09° for the quadratic model, compared to 5°–6° for the nearest-neighbor method (purple).

sections.heading: Step-by-Step Validation: From a Rigid Plate to Human Breathing
sections.summary: Three experimental benchmarks were built to validate the framework progressively: angle-tracking accuracy on a rigid flat plate, autonomous S4C sweep search and view recovery on a cardiac phantom, and continuous S4C view tracking under free respiration on a human volunteer.
sections.details:
To rigorously evaluate performance toward clinical deployment, the framework was tested across three setups of increasing complexity.

[Tilt Tracking on a Flat Plate]
To evaluate pure geometric accuracy, the probe was pressed against a rigid flat plate. Ground-truth relative angles between the plate normal and probe axis were tracked using optical motion capture. Target tilt angles ranging from $-40^\circ$ to $+40^\circ$ in $10^\circ$ increments (8 conditions) were commanded, measuring steady-state error, standard deviation, and settling time (time to remain within $\pm 2^\circ$ of the target).

[Sweep Search and Recovery on a Cardiac Phantom]
Next, an ultrasound-guided workflow was assessed. The probe was engaged at the subcostal window of a cardiac phantom (7.2 N target force) and performed an out-of-plane pivot sweep across $30^\circ$ in $1^\circ$ steps. For each B-mode frame, a composite quality score $S_{cmp}$ was computed within a region of interest (ROI) combining Otsu's thresholding and Sobel gradient magnitude to automatically identify the optimal S4C view. The robot then returned to an initial configuration and attempted to autonomously restore the target angle based on the estimated surface normal.

[In-Vivo Tracking Under Respiration]
Finally, adaptation to physiological motion was verified on a healthy adult volunteer. An expert sonographer manually adjusted the probe to establish a clean S4C view, and the relative tilt angle to the normal was recorded as the target. The robot then initiated autonomous tracking with a 7.5 N target force, maintaining the S4C view for 60 seconds while the abdominal wall moved rhythmically under natural breathing.

sections.heading: Holding a Deep ~44-Degree Tilt Against a Breathing Abdomen
sections.summary: The flat-plate test achieved a mean angular error of 1.06°. In phantom experiments, the system recovered the optimal ~20° tilt view accurately. In in-vivo testing, it held an average non-normal tilt of 44.39° despite respiratory shifts in the surface normal, preserving a clear S4C view throughout.
sections.details:
The results clearly confirmed the framework's tracking precision and clinical applicability.

[Flat Plate Tracking Precision]
Across all eight commanded angles, the steady-state mean absolute error was $1.06 \pm 0.66^\circ$, with a maximum steady-state standard deviation of just $0.13^\circ$, demonstrating drift-free stability. Except for the $+30^\circ$ trial where settling error reached $2.49^\circ$ (slightly above the $2^\circ$ threshold), all conditions settled within 1.57 to 5.66 seconds.

[Phantom Search and Recovery]
During the sweep phase, the clearest 4-chamber view with the maximum composite score was identified at 11.94 s (base tilt $25.19^\circ$, normal-relative tilt $\approx 20^\circ$). In the recovery phase starting from a near-normal posture, the robot successfully restored the target orientation to a relative tilt of $\approx 18^\circ$ by the final frame (26.94 s). Contact force was kept at $7.34 \pm 0.61$ N against the 7.2 N command, reliably reproducing the chamber structures on ultrasound.

[In-Vivo Respiratory Tracking]
Over the 60-second trial (900 frames), the expert-defined target tilt relative to the normal was $41.20^\circ$. During the tracking window after initial contact, the measured normal-relative tilt was maintained at a mean of $44.39 \pm 2.59^\circ$ (range: 39.02°–51.00°). Notably, while the body surface normal in the robot base frame oscillated periodically due to respiration, the probe's angle relative to the normal stayed nearly constant. This proves that the robot actively compensated for surface movement rather than holding a rigid pose. Contact force averaged $6.42 \pm 1.98$ N, keeping the S4C anatomical plane visible without interruption.

(b) Force profile (7.2 N target), normal-relative tilt angle, base-frame surface normal, and image metrics, confirming accurate recovery of the target tilt (~18°–20°) after returning to the initial pose.

In the middle plot of (b), the base-frame surface normal (green) oscillates cyclically with breathing, while the probe's normal-relative tilt angle (blue) remains confined within a narrow band around 44°, demonstrating active tracking of the moving body surface.

sections.heading: From Base Frame to Surface Frame: A New Benchmark for Robotic US
sections.summary: This study proves that robotic ultrasound orientation must be defined relative to the dynamic local surface normal rather than the robot base frame. While further trials and clinical image metrics are needed, it marks a significant step toward practical autonomous ultrasound.
sections.details:
The core contribution of this work is a paradigm shift in probe orientation control. By moving past the conventional constraint of surface-normal positioning, the authors enabled omni-directional tracking relative to real-time local surface normals. This allows robotic systems to automatically capture and retain oblique clinical imaging planes, like the S4C view, which were previously difficult to automate.

The authors also note several limitations. First, in-vivo validation was conducted on a single healthy volunteer; broader clinical studies across diverse body types and anatomies remain necessary. Second, the composite image score used in phantom experiments served as an empirical heuristic for geometric reproducibility, not an accredited clinical image quality metric. Third, the in-vivo study evaluated angle retention from an expert-selected pose rather than autonomous online sweep optimization, as optimal force and positioning vary complexly with patient acoustic windows and tissue thickness.

Future work will focus on multi-subject clinical trials, diverse anatomical views, and integrating direct visual servoing from B-mode ultrasound with hybrid position-orientation-force control.

takeaways: In robotic ultrasound, defining and controlling probe orientation relative to the dynamic local surface normal—rather than a fixed robot base frame—is essential for retaining clinical imaging views.
Fitting a quadratic surface to local skin point clouds captures natural body curvature while filtering out sensor noise, providing analytical, stable surface normals in just ~0.1 ms.

A hierarchical task-space controller effectively balances probe surface contact (in-plane orthogonality), non-normal target tilt, and probe axial rotation constraints to keep diagnostic cross-sections intact.
limitations: In-vivo validation was limited to a single subject; the impact of varying body mass index, subcutaneous tissue thickness, and skeletal variations on surface modeling and tracking accuracy has yet to be comprehensively studied.
The in-vivo experiment evaluated retention of an expert-defined tilt angle rather than executing an end-to-end, image-driven autonomous view optimization sweep.
The image quality metric used in phantom trials (Otsu thresholding plus Sobel gradient) is an empirical search heuristic rather than a validated clinical ultrasound quality assessment standard.
